title: Contrasting Patterns of Cortical Volume Change in First-Episode Schizophrenia-Spectrum Psychosis
abstract: Importance Average gray matter volume (GMV) loss in early psychosis may conceal clinically relevant differences in brain change. Objective To identify longitudinal GMV-change patterns, their cross-site correspondence, and clinical associations. Design, Setting, and Participants Prospective cohort with T1-weighted MRI acquired during 2011–2026 at 2 Czech sites; median follow-up, approximately 13 months. Participants were 222 patients with first-episode schizophrenia-spectrum psychosis and 178 healthy controls frequency-matched by site and baseline age. Exposure First-episode psychosis vs healthy control status. Main Outcomes and Measures Diagnosis-blind clustering by site of image-quality-corrected, subsequently annualized GMV change across 333 cortical parcels; longitudinal voxel-based morphometry (VBM); Global Assessment of Functioning and consensus 5-factor Positive and Negative Syndrome Scale negative-symptom scores. Results Among 400 participants (mean [SD] age, 28.2 [7.5] years), 208 (52.0%) were male. Each site independently yielded 3 clusters: C1 (near-stable GMV), C2 (pronounced decrease), and C3 (increase). Cross-site centroid correlations across 333 parcels were strong for C2 and C3 (Spearman ρ = 0.865 and 0.861); C1 correlation was weak (ρ = 0.138), as expected for near-zero profiles with little regional variation. C2/C3 correspondence supported pooling matched site-specific clusters for post hoc analyses. Pooled clusters contained 77 patients and 125 controls in C1, 66 patients and 16 controls in C2, and 79 patients and 37 controls in C3. Suffixes −P and −HC identify patient and control subgroups. To situate patient changes relative to controls, post hoc VBM revealed an unanticipated gradient of increasingly pronounced GMV reduction across C1-HC → C1-P → C2-P, prominently involving association cortex, and bilateral ventral temporal GMV increase in C3-P (familywise error–corrected P < .05). The opposite contrast along this ordering showed periventricular changes consistent with progressively greater ventricular enlargement. C2-P had the lowest mean follow-up functioning and highest mean negative-symptom severity (adjusted omnibus P = .005 and .02); clinical changes from baseline did not differ significantly among patient groups. Conclusions and Relevance Early GMV change in psychosis was not uniform but comprised two contrasting directions: a clinically relevant, control-anchored pattern of increasingly pronounced GMV loss involving default mode regions and a distinct, directionally opposing ventral temporal increase. Average gray matter volume (GMV) loss in early psychosis may conceal clinically relevant differences in brain change.

Objective

To identify longitudinal GMV-change patterns, their cross-site correspondence, and clinical associations.

Prospective cohort with T1-weighted MRI acquired during 2011–2026 at 2 Czech sites; median follow-up, approximately 13 months. Participants were 222 patients with first-episode schizophrenia-spectrum psychosis and 178 healthy controls frequency-matched by site and baseline age.

Exposure

First-episode psychosis vs healthy control status.

Diagnosis-blind clustering by site of image-quality-corrected, subsequently annualized GMV change across 333 cortical parcels; longitudinal voxel-based morphometry (VBM); Global Assessment of Functioning and consensus 5-factor Positive and Negative Syndrome Scale negative-symptom scores.

Among 400 participants (mean [SD] age, 28.2 [7.5] years), 208 (52.0%) were male. Each site independently yielded 3 clusters: C1 (near-stable GMV), C2 (pronounced decrease), and C3 (increase). title: Age-, sex-, and ethnicity-stratified CMR strain reference ranges and centile-based categories from the Healthy Hearts Consortium
abstract: Background This study presents reference ranges for cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR)-derived myocardial strain from the Healthy Hearts Consortium, while evaluating variations by demographic characteristics (age, sex, and ethnicity) and technical factors (scanner vendor, magnetic field strength). We derived reference ranges and centile-based categories for ventricular, atrial, and rapid strain parameters. The prognostic relevance of these categories was assessed by examining their associations with incident cardiovascular events. Methods The dataset included 9,088 CMR studies. Automated image analysis pipelines were established using suiteHEART (NeoSoft Inc.) and cvi42 (Circle Cardiovascular Imaging). A three-step quality control framework was applied including exclusion of incomplete data, visual assessment of image and segmentation quality, and statistical outlier removal. Ventricular strain and strain rate were measured using both software solutions. Additional cvi42-derived metrics included velocity and displacement, annular plane systolic excursion metrics, and rapid strain parameters. Age- and sex-specific reference ranges were generated using lambda–mu–sigma (LMS) modeling with penalized splines. Reference ranges were defined as values between the 2.5 th and 97.5 th percentiles. For lower-tail classification, values below the 2.5th percentile were considered mildly out-of-range and values below the 0.5th percentile at least moderately out-of-range. Differences across scanner vendors (Siemens, Philips, GE) and magnetic field strengths (1.5 T vs. 3 T) were evaluated using adjusted linear models. The prognostic relevance of selected cvi42-derived categories was evaluated in approximately 45,000 UK Biobank participants using Cox regression adjusted for age, sex, and body mass index. Results After quality control, 8,975 CMR examinations (cvi42) and 8,992 (suiteHEART) were available for analysis; these represent software-specific analytic cohorts. Most exclusions occurred during visual quality control. Women had higher absolute ventricular and atrial strain values than men across all age groups. Left ventricular (LV) longitudinal strain and strain rate were slightly lower in older ages, whereas circumferential and radial parameters remained largely stable. Left atrial strain was also lower in older age groups, while right atrial strain did not vary by age. Annular plane systolic excursion and rapid strain metrics showed similar sex-specific patterns, with modestly lower atrial and displacement values in older groups. Ethnicity-related differences were modest, heterogeneous, and substantially smaller in magnitude than age- and sex-related differences. Technical effects were parameter specific. While LV longitudinal and circumferential strains were largely unaffected, radial strain was higher at 3 T and showed vendor-related differences. LMS-derived reference ranges and centile thresholds were applied both across all ethnicities and within ethnicity-specific analyses, and are presented stratified by age and sex. In the prognostic analysis, centile categories were most consistently associated with incident heart failure. LV longitudinal, circumferential, and radial strain below the 0.5th centile were associated with significantly increased risk of incident heart failure (HRs: 9.9 to 12.4, 95% CIs 7.00–13.90 to 8.49–18.06). Conclusion This study provides age- and sex-specific reference ranges and centile-based categories for CMR-derived strain parameters in a large reference population. Age and sex represent the primary determinants of myocardial deformation, whereas scanner-related effects are parameter-specific. Values in the lower extremes of the healthy reference distribution, particularly for LV strain, are associated with increased risk of incident heart failure. These findings enable standardized, centile-based classification of myocardial strain, facilitating consistent interpretation and improving risk stratification in research and clinical practice.

title: SCORES (Selection of Clinical Observations for Risk Evaluation Scores): Impact of Heart Rate Selection on Simplified Geneva Score Performance in Suspected Pulmonary Embolism
abstract: Background The Simplified Geneva Score (SGS) incorporates two heart-rate thresholds. Multiple heart-rate measurements are commonly recorded during emergency department (ED) assessment. While the original SGS specifies use of mean heart rate, real-world implementation is unlikely to reflect this, and the effect of alternative heart-rate selection methods on score performance is unknown. Methods SCORES was a retrospective within-subject study of consecutive ED patients at a single urban hospital undergoing computed tomography pulmonary angiography (CTPA) for suspected pulmonary embolism (PE). Four SGS variants were calculated using the first, highest, mean, and lowest recorded pre-CTPA heart rate. Outcomes included score output, risk classification, diagnostic performance, reclassification flow, and downstream imaging utilisation. Precision estimates and comparisons were derived using empirical resampling techniques. Results 590 episodes were reviewed with 581 included for analysis. PE was confirmed in 50 cases (8.6%). Mean SGS differed significantly across all heart-rate implementations (p<0.0001). The proportion classified as high risk varied from 15% using the lowest heart rate to 40% using the highest heart rate. Reclassification across the SGS threshold was common, with 25% of episodes changing risk category unidirectionally between lowest and highest heart rate implementations. SGS(lowest HR) compared with SGS(mean HR) and SGS(highest HR) demonstrated higher specificity (87.6% vs 73.4% vs 62.1%), improved AUROC (0.744 vs 0.704 vs 0.659), and reduced downstream CTPA utilisation (818 vs 876 vs 920 scans per 100 PEs diagnosed), with no additional pulmonary emboli missed within the complete diagnostic pathway. Conclusions Heart-rate selection materially influences SGS output, risk classification, diagnostic performance, and imaging utilisation. In this retrospective cohort, use of the lowest recorded heart rate produced the most favourable overall balance of discrimination and diagnostic efficiency, supporting prospective validation.

title: Senescence-induced Spatio-temporal Re-organization of the Nuclear Lamina Dynamic Landscape at Single-molecule Level in Live Human RPE Cells
abstract: ABSTRACT A defining hallmark of cellular senescence is the extensive remodeling of the nuclear lamina (NL) in both structure, composition, and its interactions with lamina-associated genomic domains. However, how such senescence-induced changes could quantitatively impact the spatio-temporal dynamics of NL interactions at the single-molecule level remain poorly understood. Herein, using human retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells as model system, we establish a robust, chemically inducible cellular senescence model capable of recapitulating key signatures of the senescence-associated phenotype. Senescent RPE cells exhibit distinct alteration patterns in the expression of various NL components, including lamin B receptor (LBR) and emerin, two key mediators of NL– chromatin interactions. Importantly, live-cell diffusion measurements via imaging FCS reveal globally enhanced mobility for both LBR and emerin, indicative of weakened NL anchoring in senescent cells. Single-molecule tracking and super-resolved STAR mapping further unveil distinct, multi-modal re-organization of their NL-binding dynamics in both space and time (especially in the form of LBR binding “hotspots” where multiple stable binding events cluster to effect more extended and prolonged interaction), in line with their respective expression-level alterations and differential lamin interactions. Moreover, correlative mapping uncovers a strong spatial coupling between reduced LBR mobility and highly condensed constitutive heterochromatin domains at the NL, which become dispersed during senescence. Collectively, these findings demonstrate the re-organization of NL dynamic landscape at single-molecule level as a critical and previously under-explored facet of senescence-induced NL remodeling, and point to a synergistic interplay between physical de-anchoring, dynamic attenuation of stable NL-binding and spatial restructuring of chromatin architecture in modulating NL–heterochromatin contacts to potentially effect global changes in senescence-associated gene expression. STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE In this study, we combine a suite of quantitative imaging and transcriptomic profiling approaches with complementary capabilities and perform, to our knowledge, the first rigorous characterization of the impact of cellular senescence on the spatio-temporal dynamics of NL interactions at the single-molecule level in live human cells. Our findings not only reveal a key and previously overlooked dimension of NL remodeling during cellular senescence, but also shed first-of-its-kind quantitative insights into a mechanism by which the multi-modal binding landscape at the NL work in concert with higher-order chromatin architecture and NL–chromatin anchoring to modulate the contacts between NL and heterochromatin, which can in turn alter the global gene expression program to drive senescence.

title: Integration of Neuroimaging and Histopathology in a Squirrel Monkey Model of Spontaneous Cerebral Amyloid Angiopathy and Amyloid-Related Imaging Abnormalities
abstract: Cerebral amyloid angiopathy (CAA) is a prevalent cerebrovascular pathology in AD and contributes to amyloid-related imaging abnormalities (ARIA), a major complication of current anti-amyloid immunotherapy. Despite its growing clinical importance, critical gaps remain in the development of reliable biomarkers for antemortem diagnosis of CAA. Squirrel monkeys (SQMs) are a valuable non-human primate model with translational relevance due to their universal propensity to develop abundant CAA and spontaneous ARIA in geriatric animals. The present study employed R 2 *, the apparent transverse relaxation rate, which is sensitive to susceptibility-related tissue properties, including iron content and blood oxygenation levels, to monitor age-related brain pathology in SQMs with varying CAA severity. Young, early geriatric, and late geriatric SQMs underwent 7T MRI using a dual-purpose T 2 *-w 3D multi-gradient-echo sequence for high-resolution anatomy and quantitative R 2 * mapping, alongside T 2 -w/FLAIR imaging. Whole-brain and gray matter R 2 * increased with age. In contrast, white matter R 2 * showed an initial increase followed by a late-life reversal, likely reflecting age-related changes in myelin integrity, tissue microstructure, and tissue water content. MRI-histopathology correlation linked T 2 *-w MRI hypointensities to CAA-positive iron-laden vessels associated with perivascular inflammation and, in some cases, hemosiderin deposits. Here we confirmed the occurrence of ARIA-H and ARIA-E events in geriatric animals. SQMs provided a valuable opportunity to examine the underlying pathology of spontaneous ARIA-E, revealing distinctive tissue signatures associated with its manifestation. ARIA-E hyperintensities were characterized by reactive gliosis and BBB disruption, whereas more advanced lesions exhibited perivascular lymphocytic infiltration and evidence of myelin and axonal injury. The current study presents compelling evidence linking R 2 * alterations with CAA severity and ARIA-related tissue injury, providing a foundation for further advancing early detection of CAA, ARIA risk assessment, and treatment strategies.

title: Autoencoder-based anomaly mapping and visualization of white matter deformation with application to glioma cases
abstract: Introduction Gliomas can alter white matter pathways, causing structural deformation and functional impairments. However, there is no method to map these structural alterations across the whole brain to support diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment planning. To address this gap, we propose a novel framework based on a convolutional autoencoder that learns geometry-preserving streamline embeddings for mapping structural connectivity anomalies Methods We trained and validated the autoencoder on 100 million synthetic streamlines and evaluated the anomaly-mapping pipeline using data from 118 healthy subjects. We analyzed how different tractography algorithms affect anomaly scores and demonstrated its feasibility in five glioma patients using multi-shell and single-shell diffusion MRI. Results Latent-space distances strongly associated with native-space geometric distances ( R ² = 0.82–0.98), supporting preserved streamline geometry in the learned embeddings. Anomaly scores varied with both the input and reference tractography methods. Patient anomaly maps showed elevated scores near gliomas and extending distally along affected pathways. These whole-brain anomaly maps were generated within minutes. Conclusion The framework offers a practical way to quantify and visualize geometric deviations in whole-brain tractograms, providing novel insights beyond current network and microstructural analyses, with relevance to clinical applications where white matter deformation is pertinent.

title: A large, comprehensive labeled MRI dataset of the human lateral ventricle choroid plexus
abstract: The choroid plexus (ChP) is a highly vascularized structure located in the brain ventricles that plays important roles in multiple central nervous system functions. ChP enlargement has been implicated in many neuropsychiatric conditions such as multiple sclerosis, depression, schizophrenia, and Alzheimer’s disease. However, limitation in the accuracy of the current segmentation tools highlight the need for more reliable methods to quantify ChP volume in healthy and clinical human populations. The shape and size of the ChP vary drastically from person to person, and currently there are no large ChP datasets which allow comprehensive training of segmentation models. Here we introduce DataPlex, a collection of 700 structural MRI brain images where the lateral ventricle ChP has been manually labeled and checked by expert human raters. DataPlex is balanced and representative across a wide range of scanning parameters, demographics, and clinical profiles, and subject-level information will be available for each labeled image. DataPlex will be open source to support the creation of reliable segmentation tools for the human lateral ventricle ChP.

title: Ascending Aortic Calcium Identifies Patients at Risk Despite Normal Myocardial Flow, Perfusion and Coronary Calcium: A 13-Site Cohort Study
abstract: Background Patients with normal perfusion, normal myocardial flow reserve (MFR) and no coronary artery calcium (CAC) on myocardial perfusion imaging are considered low risk. Yet, adverse events still occur and no routinely reported imaging marker stratifies residual risk. This study aims to determine whether fully automated ascending aortic calcification (AAC) from the attenuation correction CT stratifies risk in these patients. Methods In the multicenter REFINE-PET registry, AAC was quantified from non-contrast CT using deep learning aortic segmentation and Agatston scoring. Triple-normal was defined as stress total perfusion deficit (TPD) <5%, MFR >2 and CAC 0. The primary endpoint was cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction or heart failure admission, with heart failure admission as key secondary endpoint. Cox models were adjusted for clinical confounders. Results Of 21,923 patients, 3,580 (16.3%) were triple-normal, of whom 1,322 (36.9%) had AAC (median Agatston 65, IQR 22-212). Agreement with three blinded readers was good to excellent (Intraclass correlation coefficient 0.87-0.90). Over a median follow-up of 52 months (IQR 26-69), 194 primary events occurred. Per standard deviation, AAC was independently associated with the primary endpoint (adjusted HR 1.24, 95% CI 1.09-1.40; p<0.001), heart failure admission (adjusted HR 1.30, 95% CI 1.10-1.55; p=0.003) and all-cause mortality (adjusted HR 1.17, 95% CI 1.04-1.32; p=0.009). AAC improved model fit beyond clinical factors, MFR and TPD (p≤0.009), with modest gains in discrimination (ΔC 0.007-0.009). Conclusions In patients with normal PET readouts, automated AAC was independently associated with adverse outcomes, most strongly heart failure admission, beyond clinical risk factors, perfusion and flow. Clinical Perspective What Is New? In 3,580 patients with normal perfusion, normal myocardial flow reserve and no coronary artery calcium on PET, more than one in three had ascending aortic calcification on the attenuation correction CT. Ascending aortic calcification was independently associated with cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction or heart failure admission (adjusted hazard ratio per SD 1.24, 95% CI 1.09-1.40), most strongly with heart failure admission. A fast, fully automated method scored ascending aortic calcification with agreement to expert readers similar to agreement between readers. What Are the Clinical Implications? A normal perfusion PET with normal flow and no coronary calcium does not mean uniformly low risk when the ascending aorta is calcified. Because ascending aortic calcification is scored automatically from the CT acquired with every perfusion PET, it could be reported routinely without additional scanning, cost or radiation. Patients presumed low risk who have ascending aortic calcification may warrant heart failure-oriented prevention, such as natriuretic peptide screening, pending prospective validation.

Per standard deviation, AAC was independently associated with the primary endpoint (adjusted HR 1.24, 95% CI 1.09-1.40; p<0.001), heart failure admission (adjusted HR 1.30, 95% CI 1.10-1.55; p=0.003) and all-cause mortality (adjusted HR 1.17, 95% CI 1.04-1.32; p=0.009). AAC improved model fit beyond clinical factors, MFR and TPD (p≤0.009), with modest gains in discrimination (ΔC 0.007-0.009).

Conclusions

In patients with normal PET readouts, automated AAC was independently associated with adverse outcomes, most strongly heart failure admission, beyond clinical risk factors, perfusion and flow.

Clinical Perspective

What Is New?

In 3,580 patients with normal perfusion, normal myocardial flow reserve and no coronary artery calcium on PET, more than one in three had ascending aortic calcification on the attenuation correction CT. Ascending aortic calcification was independently associated with cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction or heart failure admission (adjusted hazard ratio per SD 1.24, 95% CI 1.09-1.40), most strongly with heart failure admission. A fast, fully automated method scored ascending aortic calcification with agreement to expert readers similar to agreement between readers.

What Are the Clinical Implications?

A normal perfusion PET with normal flow and no coronary calcium does not mean uniformly low risk when the ascending aorta is calcified. Because ascending aortic calcification is scored automatically from the CT acquired with every perfusion PET, it could be reported routinely without additional scanning, cost or radiation. Patients presumed low risk who have ascending aortic calcification may warrant heart failure-oriented prevention, such as natriuretic peptide screening, pending prospective validation.

title: Normative transcriptomic clues to thalamic developmental vulnerability in C9orf7 2-FTLD
abstract: C9orf72 encodes a protein that is important for both typical neurodevelopment and homeostatic processes across the lifespan. Pathogenic C9orf72 repeat expansions constitute the most common genetic cause of frontotemporal lobar degeneration (FTLD). Collectively, preclinical models and clinical neuroimaging studies have observed smaller thalamic volumes in C9orf72 -associated FTLD, including in asymptomatic young adult C9orf72 repeat expansion carriers across 18 to 30 years old, supportive of potential neurodevelopmental origins. However, it is unknown whether asymptomatic young adult C9orf72 expansion carriers demonstrate volume differences in specific thalamic nuclei, as reported in older asymptomatic carriers and symptomatic patients; if so, normative transcriptomic patterns could reveal relevant neurodevelopmental and/or FTLD-related neurodegenerative processes. This study investigated volumetric MRI differences of the thalamic nuclei in asymptomatic young adult C9orf72 expansion carriers compared to non-carriers, and examined spatial associations with normative thalamic transcriptomics from 8 weeks post-conception through middle age. Young adult C9orf72 expansion carriers ( n =72) and non-carriers ( n =48) were enrolled in the Frontotemporal Dementia Prevention Initiative across Europe, Canada, and the USA (ages: 18-30 years; sex: 57% female). Spatial associations between young adult thalamic nuclei volumes and normative transcriptomics from the Allen Human Brain Atlas were examined using complementary data-driven and hypothesis-driven approaches. Spatial expression patterns of transcripts of interest were characterized across prenatal and postnatal neurodevelopment using BrainSpan data. Smaller volumes of the pulvinar, mediodorsal, and lateral nuclei were observed in young adult C9orf72 expansion carriers compared to non-carriers. These nuclei showed higher normative expression of transcripts involved concurrently in neurodevelopmental and C9orf72 -associated FTLD neurodegenerative processes (including lysosomal, autophagic, and small GTPase functions), and lower normative expression of CALB1 , a marker of prenatal human thalamic development. Normative expression of CALB2 (another human thalamic development marker) yielded positive correlations with C9orf72 across prenatal development to adulthood. These findings identify candidate transcripts that may provide insight into the molecular architecture leading to smaller thalamic nuclei volumes in C9orf72 -associated FTLD.

title: Population-based Ethnoracial Disparity in Life’s Essential 8 Vascular Health, Cerebral Small Vessel Disease & Cognition
abstract: Background Whether ethnoracial differences in cerebral small vessel disease (cSVD) appear in multimarker burden, particular MRI manifestations, or both, and how they relate to Life’s Essential 8 (LE8) cardiovascular health and cognition, is unclear. Methods This cross-sectional study included 44,982 participants and an age- and sex-matched subsample of 1,426 with reviewed lacune and cerebral microbleed (CMB) ratings. White, South Asian, Black, Chinese and Mixed participants were compared on 0–2 (white matter hyperintensity [WMH]/enlarged perivascular space [ePVS]) and 0–4 (adding CMB and lacunes) composite scores and each marker. LE8 was related to WMH and composite burden, and cognitive means were compared by group. Models were age-, sex- and center-adjusted with false-discovery-rate correction. Results Both composite scores differed across groups (0–2: P=0.00010; 0–4: P=0.0011), with greater burden in Black than South Asian (0–4: OR 1.66; 95% CI, 1.21–2.28) and Chinese participants (OR 2.36; 1.51–3.70), whereas Black–White contrasts were not detected. Black participants had higher WMH volume than White participants (β=0.209; 0.110–0.308), robust to deprivation adjustment and segmentation method; South Asian participants had fewer ePVS (0.82; 0.72–0.93). No ethnoracial-group differences in lacune or CMB counts were detected after correction. Higher LE8 was associated with lower WMH volume (β=−0.13 per SD; −0.17 to −0.09) and lower two-marker burden (OR 0.89 per SD; 0.87–0.91) without detected ethnoracial moderation. Black participants, who had the least favorable LE8 scores, and South Asian participants had lower global cognition than White participants (z −0.76 and −0.57 versus 0.24) despite differing WMH profiles; the pooled WMH–cognition association was null. Conclusions Ethnoracial differences in multimarker cSVD burden were evident but marker-dependent: WMH showed the clearest Black–White difference; focal-lesion contrasts were inconclusive. Better cardiovascular health related to lower WMH and aggregate cSVD burden across groups, whereas cognitive differences did not track cSVD burden, supporting prospective prevention and cognition studies.

title: A defined multi-kingdom microbial consortium naturalizes the immune system of laboratory mice
abstract: Dirty mice experiments suggest that laboratory mice fail to model certain human immune responses due to their limited microbial exposure. The identity, nature, and number of microbes required to normalize the immune system are unknown. Through systematic screening, we uncovered unexpected cross-kingdom microbial interactions and identified four enteric microbes spanning viruses, fungi, and protists sufficient to reproduce key immunological features of pet store mice and adult humans. This consortium also altered cancer outcomes, shifting tumorigenesis toward the anatomical pattern of human familial adenomatous polyposis in ApcMin/+ mice and recapitulating the imperfect response of many patients to chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cell therapy. Thus, surprisingly few microbes can profoundly reshape immune states and disease responses, providing a tractable approach to naturalize laboratory mouse immunity.

title: In Silico Metrological Assessment of 2D ROI Sampling Error Versus Whole-Organ 3D Volumetric CT Attenuation in Hepatic Steatosis: A Multicenter Monte Carlo Simulation on 971 Scans
abstract: PurposeTo quantify the metrological sampling error of conventional 2D regions of interest (ROIs) relative to whole-organ 3D volumetric CT attenuation ground truth in opportunistic screening for hepatic steatosis, and to evaluate its functional dependency on intraparenchymal spatial heterogeneity. Materials and MethodsIn this retrospective computational investigation adhering to CLAIM and TRIPOD-AI reporting standards, 971 non-contrast and contrast-enhanced abdominal CT examinations were analyzed across a multicenter derivation cohort (TotalSegmentator v2, n = 841) and an external validation cohort (Medical Segmentation Decathlon Task03 Liver, n = 130). Automated 3D liver segmentation was conducted using nnU-Net, supplemented by an 8-mm spherical 3D morphological erosion to eliminate peripheral partial volume effects, liver capsule artifacts, and major hilar vascular structures. Three clinical sampling paradigms (1, 3, and 5 axial circular 2D ROIs of 15 mm diameter) were simulated through 500 stochastic Monte Carlo iterations per examination (485,500 total simulations). Absolute metrological sampling error (|{Delta}HU| = |HU_ROI - HU_3D|) and diagnostic steatosis misclassification rates at the standard unenhanced threshold (HU_3D [≤] 40 HU) were evaluated. Statistical significance across sampling paradigms was tested using two-tailed paired Wilcoxon signed-rank tests. ResultsIn the derivation cohort (n = 841), the conventional guideline-recommended 3-ROI paradigm yielded a mean absolute sampling error of 6.61 {+/-} 7.83 HU (median: 2.92 HU; interquartile range: 1.34-8.45 HU). While representing a 41.6% error reduction compared to the single-ROI approach (11.32 {+/-} 14.16 HU; W = 0, p < 0.001), it demonstrated significant residual error compared to the extended 5-ROI approach (5.21 {+/-} 6.00 HU; W = 8, p < 0.001). Intraparenchymal spatial heterogeneity ({sigma}_HU) strongly predicted sampling error (Pearson r = 0.850, 95% CI: 0.830-0.868, p < 0.001). In borderline attenuation zones (35-45 HU), diagnostic misclassification reached 45.2% in heterogeneous livers. Findings were replicated in the external validation cohort (mean |{Delta}HU| = 7.38 HU for 1 ROI vs. 5.14 HU for 3 ROIs, p < 0.001). ConclusionManual 2D ROI sampling exhibits an inherent physical uncertainty that exceeds the 5-HU clinical tolerance threshold in parenchymally heterogeneous livers, misclassifying nearly half of borderline examinations. Accurate opportunistic steatosis screening requires transition to automated whole-organ 3D volumetric CT densitometry embedded in PACS networks. KEY POINTSO_LIConventional 3-ROI sampling leaves an average metrological error of 6.61 {+/-} 7.83 HU compared with 3D whole-liver ground truth. C_LIO_LIIntraparenchymal spatial heterogeneity is the primary determinant of 2D sampling error (r = 0.850, p < 0.001). C_LIO_LIIn borderline diagnostic attenuation ranges (35-45 HU), 2D manual sampling misclassifies up to 45.2% of patients with spatial heterogeneity. C_LI

title: 5-HT1A Antagonist WAY-100635 Prevents Chronic Neurodegeneration and Immune Activation After TBI
abstract: ABSTRACT Traumatic brain injury (TBI) initiates secondary neurodegeneration that compromises interconnected neural circuits and contributes to persistent visual and neurobehavioral impairment. Pharmacological strategies that preserve vulnerable neurons and synapses while limiting chronic neuroinflammation remain an unmet therapeutic need. We previously identified the serotonin 1A receptor (5-HT1A) antagonist WAY-100635 through screening human stem cell-derived retinal ganglion cells (RGCs) and demonstrated that it promotes neuroprotection through cyclic adenosine monophosphate-dependent mitochondrial biogenesis. Here, we investigated whether post-injury treatment extends this neuroprotective efficacy to cerebral and visual circuitry following TBI. Male C57BL/6J mice aged 2-3 months underwent unilateral controlled cortical impact (CCI) involving the left visual cortex. Mice were randomly assigned to sham, untreated injury or treated injury groups, with 3-10 sham controls and 5-8 mice per injury group across experiments. WAY-100635 was administered intraperitoneally at 5 mg/kg daily, beginning 1 hour after injury and continuing for 6 weeks. Therapeutic efficacy was assessed using motor and psychological-health-relevant risk-taking/behavioral disinhibition by elevated-plus-maze assessment, visual electrophysiology, optokinetic responses, diffusion magnetic resonance imaging, and retinal and cortical histopathology. Unilateral cortical injury produced bilateral RGC dysfunction and loss, with greater degeneration in the eye contralateral to the injured hemisphere, consistent with predominantly crossed murine visual projections. WAY-100635 significantly preserved RGC survival and function, improved visual acuity and contrast sensitivity, and preserved visually evoked cortical responses to contralateral eye stimulation. Diffusion MRI revealed bilateral visual pathway abnormalities, with treatment selectively normalizing fractional anisotropy and radial kurtosis in the optic tract ipsilateral to cortical injury. In perilesional cortex, treatment preserved neuronal cell bodies and synapses detected by synaptophysin immunoreactivity while markedly reducing microglial/macrophage activation and reactive astrogliosis. These effects were accompanied by improved early motor performance and attenuation of injury-associated increases in open-arm exploration in the elevated plus maze. Cortical cavity volume was not significantly reduced, supporting preferential protection of vulnerable circuitry surrounding and connected to the primary lesion. These findings identify post-injury WAY-100635 treatment as a novel therapeutic intervention that combines neuronal and synaptic preservation with reduced chronic glial activation and improved functional outcomes. They support further translational development of serotonin 1A receptor antagonism to limit secondary neurodegeneration and the visual and neurobehavioral consequences of TBI. Graphical Abstract

title: Ex-vivo 7T MRI for accurate margin assessment in oral squamous cell carcinoma surgery
abstract: IntroductionResection margins in oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC) are frequently inadequate. This study investigated the accuracy and diagnostic performance of ex-vivo 7T MRI against histology. MethodsFifty OSCC specimens underwent ex-vivo 7T MRI. Tumours were segmented on corresponding histology and twice on MRI: blinded to histology (radiologist segmentation; clinical practice) and using histology (histology-MR segmentation; MR-based ground truth). Resection margins were measured in five regions and compared with histology. ResultsAnterior and posterior margins were generally smaller on MRI than on histology (maximum mean difference -2.5 mm), whereas cranial, caudal and deep margins were generally larger on MRI (mean differences <1 mm). For close margins (<5 mm), sensitivity was 95% for histology-MR segmentations and 91% for radiologist segmentations, with 75% specificity for both. ConclusionEx-vivo 7T MRI accurately measures resection margins and detects close margins with high sensitivity. A future clinical trial will determine whether intraoperative implementation reduces inadequate margins and adjuvant treatment.

title: MRI Biomarkers for Brain Metastases in Lung Cancer Using Machine Learning
abstract: Purpose Existing prognostic models for brain metastases from lung cancer rely on clinical variables and do not capture the biological heterogeneity of host or tumor factors underlying survival outcomes. We evaluated whether MRI-derived radiomic biomarkers improve prognostic stratification beyond clinical variables. We also investigated their biological correlates using matched histopathology. Experimental Design This retrospective study included 103 patients with brain metastases from lung cancer and matched pre-operative MRI and histopathology. Radiomic features from T1-weighted contrast-enhanced and T2-weighted fluid-attenuated inversion recovery sequences were combined with clinical variables to train Cox proportional hazards, random survival forest, and DeepSurv models for overall survival (OS), CNS progression, and leptomeningeal (LM) progression. Risk groups from an imaging-only model were compared for clinical and histopathologic differences. Results Imaging features improved prognostic performance beyond clinical variables across all modeling frameworks, with the combined clinical-imaging DeepSurv model achieving the highest concordance index for OS (0.728). Risk groups from the best-performing model for each endpoint differed significantly in OS (median 26.7 vs. 9.1 months, p < 0.001) and LM progression ( p = 0.003), but not in CNS progression. Imaging-only risk groups did not differ significantly in any clinical variable, but high-risk patients were less likely to have tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes (46% vs. 77%, p = 0.010) and PD-L1 expression ≥ 50% (10% vs. 32%, p = 0.049). Conclusions MRI radiomic biomarkers provide prognostic information beyond established clinical variables in lung cancer brain metastases and correspond to features of the tumor immune microenvironment, supporting their potential to refine risk stratification. Statement of Translational Relevance Brain metastases affect 30-40% of patients with lung cancer. Existing prognostic models rely on clinical variables, which do not fully capture the biological heterogeneity that drives outcomes. We show that machine learning models integrating MRI-derived radiomic features with clinical variables improve prognostic discrimination beyond clinical variables alone. Because these biomarkers are derived from standard-of-care pre-operative imaging, they can be generated without additional testing or delay to treatment planning. Using matched histopathology from resected lesions, we further show that imaging-defined risk groups do not simply reproduce established clinical risk factors but instead correspond to differences in the tumor immune microenvironment, including tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes and PD-L1 expression. These findings support the use of quantitative imaging biomarkers as a non-invasive method to refine risk stratification at diagnosis, informing treatment selection and clinical trial enrollment for patients with brain metastases from lung cancer.

title: Artificial Intelligence-Based Modeling to Aid in the Identification of Genetic Conditions in Infants with Congenital Heart Disease
abstract: Background: Genetic conditions are common in congenital heart disease (CHD) and affect care, but are often missed or diagnosed late. We asked whether routine clinical data can shortlist the most likely genetic conditions. Methods: Retrospective single-center cohort of children with CHD and an echocardiogram who had either a confirmed genetic diagnosis or negative cytogenetic testing and CHD gene sequencing. Echocardiogram images and serial medical record data were added as model inputs in the order they become clinically available. Class balanced logistic regression (LR) and a multimodal deep learning fusion network were fitted to the same inputs at each step. The primary metric was balanced top-3 accuracy (correct diagnosis among the top three, averaged across conditions), with bootstrap intervals. Results: The cohort included 1,720 children (988 with common CHD-associated genetic conditions, 231 rare diagnoses, 501 negative testing). Using only inputs generated at the echocardiogram visit, LR reached a balanced top-3 accuracy 0.758 (chance 0.429). Serial records, radiology notes and ICD-10 codes, raised this to 0.809. Multimodal fusion performed similarly at each stage. With a genetic condition withheld from training, the fusion embedding placed affected children nearest to others sharing a gene group in 0.37 of cases versus 0.10 without the embedding (+0.268 [95% CI +0.242, +0.295]). Conclusions: Routine clinical data available at first echocardiogram can help identify likely genetic diagnoses, and later coded inputs ceiling. Multimodal fusion added no accuracy over LR, but places children sharing a genetic cause near one another, making nearest-neighbor retrieval informative for undiagnosed children.

title: Results of a Community-Based Coronary CT Angiography Screening in Asymptomatic Adults With Cardiovascular Risk Factors: The Broward County Heart Project
abstract: Background: Coronary CT angiography (CCTA) and calcium scoring detect subclinical coronary atherosclerosis, but the results of community based screening in asymptomatic adults with cardiovascular risk factors are poorly described. Objective. To describe the results of the first phase of a county-funded CT screening program and their variation by demographics, health system, time, and ZIP code. Methods. Retrospective analysis of aggregate reports from the Broward County Florida Heart Project (May 2023 to September 2025). Eligible residents were those with insurance coverage, age 45 to 70 years (limited exceptions), free of known cardiovascular disease and symptoms, with at least one risk factor. Examinations at six hospitals in four health systems were classified by the program team as normal (Category 1), abnormal (Category 2), or very abnormal (Category 3), with a separate flag for other non coronary abnormality. We used Wilson confidence intervals and chi square, trend, and Mantel Haenszel tests. Results. Among 7,135 participants (58.3% men; 79.0% White, 8.0% Black, 17.2% Hispanic), 43.2% had Category 1, 45.4% Category 2, and 11.4% Category 3 results; 56.8% (95% CI, 55.7% to 58.0%) had abnormal or very abnormal results. The proportion rose from 39.3% at 45 to 55 years to 78.5% at 71 or older (trend P<0.001) and was higher in men than women (68.9% vs 39.8%; odds ratio [OR], 3.36; 95% CI, 3.05 to 3.71). Rates were lower in Black than White participants (38.9% vs 58.6%; hospital adjusted OR, 0.45; 95% CI, 0.38 to 0.54) and in Hispanic than non Hispanic participants (51.0% vs 57.8%). Abnormal results ranged from 39.5% to 60.3% across health systems (P<0.001). Variation across the 50 highest volume ZIP codes did not exceed chance (P=0.53). Conclusions. More than half of insured, asymptomatic adults with risk factors screened in this community program had abnormal results, with steep age and sex gradients and unexplained variation across health systems. Black, Hispanic, and female residents were under-represented relative to the county

title: LuTuFlow: a deep learning-based pipeline for quantitative characterization of mouse lung tumors in CT imaging
abstract: Computed tomography (CT) is a widely used, non-invasive imaging tool to monitor tumor growth. Tumor identification and volumetric quantification are crucial for assessing tumor burden, whereas tracking individual tumors by aligning scans from multiple time points reveals disease progression. However, these processes remain largely dependent on manual analysis, limiting the accuracy, reproducibility, objectivity, and scalability of tumor characterization. Several deep learning models have enabled automated segmentation and object identification. However, open-source, integrated software platforms that cover the entire workflow – including processing raw CT images, annotating and tracking tumors through time, and generating data reports and visualizations – are still needed. Here, we present LuTuFlow, a computer vision pipeline incorporating a nnU-Net-based deep learning model, configured for murine lung segmentation and tumor analysis. We integrated these modules into a Napari plugin, allowing researchers to apply the entire automated workflow to transform raw CT scan datasets into quantitative readouts and interactive visualizations in a simple graphical user interface. The resulting model, iteratively refined using expert-corrected annotations, generated reliable quantitative estimates of tumor burden.

title: A Triple-Measure Model for Estimating Cranial–Brain Size Across Age Groups
abstract: Background Head circumference is widely used as an indirect indicator of brain growth and cranial capacity; however, its isolated use may lead to imprecise interpretations, particularly in borderline cases of microcephaly and megalencephaly. Complementary screening approaches that remain accessible and non-invasive may therefore be useful, especially in settings with limited access to neuroimaging. Objective To develop and evaluate an experimental, non-invasive model for estimating endocranial volume based on a combined cranial metric, termed the Triple-Measure, and to compare its performance with head circumference alone across different age ranges. Methods One hundred forensic facial approximations with known cranial scale were analyzed. Head circumference, sagittal arc, and coronal arc were measured on three-dimensional skull models, and their sum was defined as the Triple-Measure. Endocranial volume was obtained through direct segmentation of computed tomography data or by anatomical deformation of donor models. Regression analyses and validation procedures were performed, and the results were contextualized using literature-derived datasets to assess compatibility with established population parameters. Results The Triple-Measure showed a stronger correlation with endocranial volume (R = 0.83; R² = 0.69) than head circumference alone (R = 0.76; R² = 0.57), a difference confirmed by an F-test (F ≈ 17.03, p < 0.001). Validation analyses performed on independent CT cases demonstrated good agreement and consistency between predicted and measured values. The sample distribution was compatible with large population datasets derived from the literature. Based on these findings, an analog lookup table and a digital calculation tool were developed to support exploratory application across adult and developmental stages, with improved sensitivity in borderline situations. Conclusions The Triple-Measure may provide a more informative anthropometric proxy for endocranial volume than head circumference alone while remaining non-invasive and accessible. Given its exploratory nature, the method is best interpreted as a complementary screening approach intended to support clinical decision-making and to indicate when further imaging evaluation may be warranted. Additional studies with larger clinical datasets are recommended to refine its applicability across populations. Highlights Triple-measure shows improved association with endocranial volume compared to head circumference Proposed as a non-invasive, low-cost screening approach for micro- and megalencephaly Analog lookup table and digital calculator developed for exploratory and practical use Framework extended across neonatal, pediatric, and adult age groups using integrated datasets

title: MedMCP: An Open Agentic Ecosystem for Medical Imaging Workflows
abstract: Deep learning has driven rapid progress in medical image analysis, with methods for tasks such as organ segmentation, anomaly detection, and radiology report generation now matching or surpassing expert performance on several benchmarks. While many methods are released as open source, their routine adoption by clinicians and medical researchers remains limited. The bottleneck is not a lack of capable tools, but the absence of infrastructure to make them accessible to non-technical users. To break this barrier, we present MedMCP , an agentic framework that solves this last-mile problem along two axes: (1) a local agentic workspace that lets users apply state-of-the-art image analysis methods through natural language, and (2) a community-driven tool ecosystem that lets developers deploy and distribute capabilities as validated, independently testable servers. MedMCP enforces a strict orchestration-execution boundary in which a local language model translates user intent into workflow plans, while all image analysis is delegated to domain-specific tools. The framework runs entirely on-premise, every side-effecting operation passes through a human-in-the-loop permission gate, and a full provenance trail links each output to the tools, parameters, and inputs that produced it. An inspectable workspace lets users verify intermediate results rather than blindly trusting the agent, and completed sessions distill into deterministic, shareable workflows that re-execute without the agent, turning one-off interactions into reproducible analyses. This paper introduces the project’s general idea and describes the design principles that guide its development. Beyond a single toolkit, we envision MedMCP as a community-driven platform where each contributed tool becomes easily accessible, compounding individual efforts into shared capability. https://medmcp.ai https://github.com/medmcp

title: Longitudinal changes in motor network activity and connectivity in patients with suspected Transcient Ischemic Attack: an exploratory fMRI study
abstract: Background and Objectives Transient ischemic attack (TIA) diagnosis is challenging because it relies mainly on clinical assessment and exclusion of common differential. Functional MRI (fMRI) may provide a diagnostic biomarker by detecting transient brain dysfunction not visible on conventional imaging. This pilot study aimed to characterize acute motor-task BOLD activation in patients with suspected DWI-negative TIA and compare functional patterns between confirmed TIA and alternative diagnoses. Secondary objectives were to assess longitudinal changes in activation and connectivity at 3 months. Methods In this prospective single-center study, adults presenting within 24 h of transient anterior-circulation neurological symptoms underwent conventional MRI and additional motor-task fMRI. Patients with acute DWI lesions were excluded. Final diagnosis was established after 3-month follow-up. Whole-brain analyses, individualized motor cortex region-of-interest (ROI) analyses, and generalized psychophysiological interaction (gPPI) connectivity analyses were performed during the acute phase and at 3 months. Results Eight patients were enrolled; six had complete longitudinal imaging data and were included in the final analyses. Final diagnoses were TIA (n=2), migraine aura (n=2), functional neurological disorder (n=1), and hypoglycemia (n=1). Whole-brain and ROI analyses showed reduced bilateral motor-related BOLD responses during the acute phase in both TIA patients and in the patient with hypoglycemia. In contrast, patients with migraine and functional neurological disorder exhibited less marked longitudinal changes. In TIA patients, motor cortex activation increased at 3 months, tending to normalize toward values observed in non-TIA participants. Connectivity analyses revealed heterogeneous patterns, but the 2 TIA patients demonstrated increased longitudinal connectivity between the motor cortex contralateral to symptoms and other sensorimotor regions, including supplementary motor, premotor, parietal, and postcentral cortices. Discussion These preliminary findings suggest that TIA may be associated with transient bilateral reductions in motor-network activity. Functional abnormalities appeared to improve over time, supporting the hypothesis of reversible network dysfunction. Although limited by the very small sample size, this study provides the first longitudinal assessment of emergency task-based fMRI in rigorously defined TIA and supports further investigation of acute functional MRI as a potential biomarker of transient cerebral dysfunction.

title: Deep Learning and Radiomics Models for Predicting 90-Day Outcomes in Ischemic Stroke: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
abstract: BackgroundAccurate prediction of 90-day outcomes following ischemic stroke is crucial for optimizing clinical strategies. This study aimed to systematically review and meta-analyze studies using deep learning (DL) and hand-crafted radiomics (HCR) models for predicting 90-day modified Rankin Scale (mRS) outcomes after ischemic stroke. MethodsWe followed the PRISMA guidelines for systematic reviews. Four databases (PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, and Cochrane Library) were searched comprehensively for studies published up to September 2025. Inclusion criteria encompassed original research focusing on ischemic stroke patients with mRS at 90 days as the primary outcome and predictive models utilizing imaging biomarkers from CT or MRI. Quality assessment of the included studies was conducted using the PROBAST and and METhodological RadiomICs Score (METRICS) tools. ResultsSeventeen studies were included in the quantitative meta-analysis. Models demonstrated good prognostic performance for 90-day outcomes, with pooled AUCs of 0.85 (95% CI: 0.80-0.86) for internal and 0.74 (95% CI: 0.67-0.89) for external validation sets, with no significant difference (p=0.42). Deep learning and hand-crafted radiomics models showed comparable diagnostic accuracy in the primary analysis (p=0.667); a difference in sensitivity favouring hand-crafted radiomics emerged only in a post-hoc analysis after exclusion of one outlier study. Models incorporating clinical variables significantly outperformed imaging-only models (p<0.01). CT- and MRI-based models showed similar performance. Treatment-specific analyses revealed higher sensitivity for IVT-based models and higher specificity for combined MT+IVT models. ConclusionsDL and HCR models demonstrate robust potential for predicting 90-day outcomes in ischemic stroke. Future research should focus on standardizing model evaluation metrics and incorporating explainable AI techniques to improve clinical applicability.

title: Instability as Signal: Diagnosing Latent Heterogeneity in Multimodal Survival Models
abstract: Multimodal deep learning models for cancer survival prediction frequently exhibit unstable and irreproducible performance, limiting their clinical applicability. Rather than proposing a new predictive architecture, this work presents a diagnostic investigation into the sources of this instability. Using a transformer-based deep fusion model combining RNA sequencing and histopathology data from the TCGA-BRCA cohort as a diagnostic probe, we demonstrate that global survival prediction is highly unstable across data splits. We then analyze the learned multimodal embeddings in an unsupervised manner, revealing stable latent patient subgroups with significantly divergent survival outcomes. These subgroups are not explained by canonical receptor status or immune infiltration, but instead align with tumor-intrinsic proliferative activity. Conditioning survival modeling on the largest discovered subgroup recovers strong and stable prognostic performance, substantially outperforming unimodal baselines. These findings indicate that survival predictability is conditional on latent heterogeneity and suggest that heterogeneity-aware modeling strategies are essential for robust multimodal prognostication. This work establishes a methodological framework for interpreting instability in multimodal survival learning.

title: CytoLens: a modular deep learning system for quantitative cervical cytology
abstract: Cervical cytology screening relies on the visual assessment of nuclear and cellular morphology across thousands of cells per slide, a labor-intensive task that could benefit from quantitative computational support. Here we present CytoLens, a modular deep learning system that detects and counts nuclei, delineates nuclei and whole cells, measures the nuclear-to-cell area ratio (N:C), classifies cells from multifocal images and scores candidate abnormality. We trained and tested each module on a public dataset matched to its task, without pooling datasets. CytoLens detected nuclei with an F1 score of 0.931 (95% confidence interval (CI), 0.914–0.946) and counted 75 of 100 fields to within one nucleus. Point-prompted segmentation achieved mean Dice coefficients of 0.901 for nuclei and 0.847 for whole cells and, without retraining, transferred to a second dataset in which measured N:C increased with lesion grade in parallel with expert outlines. Multifocal hierarchical classification reached a mean accuracy of 0.947 across four Bethesda-aligned categories, and abnormality scores ranked annotated abnormal candidates with an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 0.865. These results support the evaluation of CytoLens on patient-linked clinical specimens.

title: CytoRipple: Mapping Tissue Polarization through Subcellular Cytoskeleton Dynamics
abstract: Spatial multi-omic technologies entail simultaneous measurement of tens-to-thousands of molecular features (e.g. RNA, protein). While cell type and state profiling is the major focus of spatial multi-omic analyses, cytoskeletal proteins are often solely utilized for cell segmentation and quality control. Here, we introduce a new computational framework, CytoRipple, that leverages these concomitant spatially-resolved single-cell measurements of cytoskeleton proteins to identify tissue-level vector fields. Polarization vectors are known to associate with cell movement and phenotype, inferring their physical orientation. We validate these associations across biological contexts and reveal how polarization vector fields can be harnessed to discover multi-cellular structures (e.g. “streams” of cells with similar polarizations). These multi-cellular cytoskeleton dynamics associate with distinct phenomena, such as vector “divergence” with CD8 + T cell activation and “streams” with spatially segmented stages of the anti-tumor immune response. Together, these data support a role for CytoRipple in revealing a dynamic layer across spatial multi-omic platforms.
originalAbstract: Spatial multi-omic technologies entail simultaneous measurement of tens-to-thousands of molecular features (e.g. RNA, protein). While cell type and state profiling is the major focus of spatial multi-omic analyses, cytoskeletal proteins are often solely utilized for cell segmentation and quality control. Here, we introduce a new computational framework, CytoRipple, that leverages these concomitant spatially-resolved single-cell measurements of cytoskeleton proteins to identify tissue-level vector fields. Polarization vectors are known to associate with cell movement and phenotype, inferring their physical orientation. We validate these associations across biological contexts and reveal how polarization vector fields can be harnessed to discover multi-cellular structures (e.g. “streams” of cells with similar polarizations). These multi-cellular cytoskeleton dynamics associate with distinct phenomena, such as vector “divergence” with CD8  + T cell activation and “streams” with spatially segmented stages of the anti-tumor immune response. Together, these data support a role for CytoRipple in revealing a dynamic layer across spatial multi-omic platforms.

title: Preoperative thymic output and T-cell repertoire diversity are associated with recurrence after nephrectomy for localized renal cell carcinoma
abstract: Radiographic thymic health and peripheral T-cell repertoire features have been linked to outcomes in renal cell carcinoma (RCC), but their prognostic value after curative-intent surgery is unclear. We quantified preoperative blood signal-joint T-cell receptor excision circles (sjTRECs), a marker of thymic output, in 218 patients with localized RCC undergoing nephrectomy and characterized T-cell receptor β (TCRβ) repertoires in 201 patients. We assessed overall survival (OS) and recurrence-free survival (RFS) using Kaplan-Meier and Cox models adjusted for age, sex, and Leibovich risk group. High sjTREC levels were associated with longer RFS after adjustment for age, sex, and Leibovich risk group (hazard ratio [HR] 0.50; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.29-0.87; p=0.015), with a concordant OS estimate (HR 0.62; 95% CI, 0.38-1.02; p=0.058). sjTREC provided additional prognostic information beyond Leibovich risk stratification for recurrence overall and among intermediate/high-risk patients (likelihood-ratio test, p=0.024 and p=0.034, respectively). Higher TCRβ diversity was associated with longer RFS overall (HR 0.76; 95% CI, 0.60-0.96; p=0.024) and among intermediate/high-risk patients with longer RFS (HR 0.71; 95% CI, 0.55-0.92; p=0.009) and OS (HR 0.80; 95% CI, 0.65-0.98; p=0.031). Preoperative sjTREC provided prognostic information beyond clinicopathological risk, with higher TCRβ diversity associated with favorable outcomes.
